records.name: Rwanda
records.current_summary:
Rwanda demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy is not criminalised, and the government formally tolerates a small LGBT presence — but a 2025 Human Rights First Rwanda Association submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents ongoing law-enforcement abuses against transgender persons, including arbitrary arrests and detentions (framed as “vagrancy” or “deviance” round-ups in Kigali's periodic street-cleaning operations). There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, and civil society operates within the regime's tight limits.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but Kigali's sweep operations can net gender-nonconforming people, and recourse is nil.
records.current_localsOnly: The sweep-detention abuses documented in the 2025 HRF submission primarily affect residents, though the sweep mechanism can catch visitors.
records.current_outOfScope: Sweep detentions are documented against trans persons specifically (2025 HRF submission).

sources.claim: Outright International Rwanda overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex intimacy is not criminalised, but the Human Rights First Rwanda Association's 2025 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents law-enforcement abuses against transgender people — harassment at identity checks and arbitrary arrests on 'vagrancy'/'public order' grounds; LGBTIQ organisations cannot register openly, a public Pride event was held in 2021, and NGO Law No. 058/2024 (adopted June 2024) raises freedom-of-association concerns.

Vice (20 Nov 2020): reports violent detentions of transgender people in Rwanda: On Christmas day in 2018, Bella was walking out of a hotel in Kigali, Rwanda’s capital city, where she had been booked to sing for the holiday. After her show, she celebrated with friends and enjoyed the afternoon at the hotel bar. Stepping onto the street to make her way home, Bella— whose name has been changed due to concerns for her safety—was stopped by police officers. “I had my service card that showed I was working ther

KT Press (25 Sep 2016): asked at Rwanda Cultural Day in San Francisco about LGBT life in Rwanda, President Kagame replied 'it hasn't been our problem. And we don't intend to make it our problem'; the piece cites Article 26 of the constitution, which recognises only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman.

Queerstory Files blog (8 Oct 2012): historical overview of the Great Lakes region — anthropologists report that same-sex relations among young Tutsi and Hutu men existed pre-colonisation but were private and secret; situates Rwanda alongside Uganda and Burundi (independence 1962) and post-1994 genocide memory. Background/history, not current visitor risk.

records.name: DR Congo
records.current_summary:
DR Congo is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct has never been criminalised — but the reality on the ground is severe insecurity: mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented, police extortion is routine, the east is an active conflict zone (M23), and LGBT organisations (Savie asbl in Bukavu) report systematic violations in their 2024 UPR submission. There is no legal gender recognition and no protection infrastructure; Kinshasa's small scene is underground.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but outing risks mob violence with no effective state protection anywhere in the country.
records.current_outOfScope: Conflict conditions in the east are general; mob justice against LGBT people is documented in UPR submissions.

sources.claim: Stakeholder submission to the DRC's 5th-cycle UPR (March 2024) by Savie asbl NGO and others: the DRC does not criminalise same-sex relations but neither protects nor promotes LGBTIQ+ rights; public displays of same-sex affection can be prosecuted under indecent-exposure provisions (Article 176 of the Penal Code: 'anyone who publicly outrages morals by actions...').

Human Rights Watch (4 Dec 2017): 120+ interviews (incl. nine Congolese security-force officers, UN officials, 21 M23 fighters) document security forces recruiting ex-M23 fighters from Uganda/Rwanda in Oct–Dec 2016 and deploying them with orders to use lethal force against protesters in Kinshasa, Goma and Lubumbashi — background on state violence and impunity in the security environment; no LGBT-specific content.

GayOut travel guide for DR Congo: rates the country 'High Risk for LGBTQ+' - no explicit national criminalisation but Article 176 ('indecent acts') and local ordinances applied to LGBTQ people; armed militia groups in eastern DRC have committed extreme violence against LGBTQ people with near-total impunity; state authority collapse means legal protections are theoretical.

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror) on LGBTQ rights in the DRC: same-sex activity legal for both sexes (never outlawed, even under Belgian rule), equal age of consent; but no gender-identity recognition, no relationship recognition (same-sex marriage banned constitutionally since 2006), limited protections; church groups promote the view that homosexuality is immoral; public same-sex affection can trigger prosecution under indecency provisions.

Queer In The World (updated 3 Dec 2023; covers both Congos): DRC-specific parts — homosexuality legal but LGBT expression censored with imprisonment exposure; violence, harassment and torture against LGBT people reported involving police, security forces and army; no legal gender change for trans people; advises visitors discretion and low profile.

freshness_all.fact: Same-sex activity legal; public-indecency provisions still occasionally used for prosecution; no anti-discrimination law — UPR-era (2025) sources remain accurate.

records.name: Haiti
records.current_summary: Haiti is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but the state has effectively collapsed: gangs control most of Port-au-Prince, the police are outgunned, and mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no LGR, no protection infrastructure, and no functioning judiciary. The trans-specific risk is inseparable from the generalised collapse — outing in gang-controlled territory can be lethal.
records.current_outOfScope: State collapse is general; mob violence against LGBT people documented.

sources.claim: Washington Blade (25 Nov 2019): Charlot Jeudy, president of Kouraj, Haiti's national LGBTQ advocacy organization, was found dead at his home in Port-au-Prince; poisoning reports were unconfirmed by the Blade. ILGALAC issued a mourning statement. The piece cites the US State Department's 2018 report that attitudes in Haiti 'remained hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity and expression, particularly in Port-au-Prince' — a direct climate warning for visibly trans visitors.

HRW World Report 2018 (Haiti chapter): LGBT persons continued to face high levels of discrimination. A June 2017 Senate bill would allow denial of the Certificat de Bonne Vie et Moeurs (a good-conduct certificate employers and universities require) on grounds of homosexuality; in August 2017 the Senate passed a bill banning same-sex marriage and public LGBT advocacy with up to 3 years' prison and a ~US$8,000 fine for parties. Both awaited a Chamber of Deputies vote as of November 2017 — status must be verified before relying on them.

freshness_all.fact: Not a criminal offence (consensual adult), but trans people exposed to vagrancy-law fines and zero protection/hate-crime coverage — current summary matches; only cited 'source' was a homepage (dead link) and should be replaced.

records.name: Vanuatu
records.current_summary: Vanuatu demands real caution. Same-sex conduct is legal (never criminalised); no LGR; small VPride community in Port Vila; kastom and church conservatism but no documented anti-trans violence pattern.

sources.claim: Sista (Oct 2016): VPride Foundation and Vanuatu Women's Centre's first joint LGBTI human-rights workshop (SPC-funded) established that same-sex partners get no protection under the Family Protection Act 2008 and must rely on penal-code routes; USP law lecturer Anita Jowitt documented only one prosecuted violence-against-lesbians case and near-invisible LGBTI court presence; VPride (est. 2014) faced church/official/chief opposition at founding.

sources.title: Vanuatu parliament amends Marriage Act to ban same-sex marriage
sources.claim: RNZ (18 Nov 2024): Parliament amended the Marriage Act to define marriage as the union of a male and a female; Internal Affairs Minister Andrew Napuat confirmed same-sex marriages cannot be registered, and pastors must not perform ceremonies against the law.

sources.title: Vanuatu moves to ban LGBTQIA+ advocacy
sources.claim: RNZ (5 Nov 2024): Ministry of Justice and Community Services to appoint a committee drafting a national policy banning LGBTQIA+ advocacy and promotion; National Human Rights coordinator Albert Nalpini said a Council of Ministers decision earlier in 2024 targeted LGBTQIA+ activities, framing V-Pride as contrary to constitutional, Christian and Melanesian values — direct risk signal for visibly LGBT/trans visitors.

records.name: Micronesia (FSM)
records.current_summary: The Federated States of Micronesia demands real caution. No federal criminalisation (some states historically had provisions); US-associated; no LGR; no documented anti-trans pattern; very thin data.

sources.claim: US State Department archived Human Rights Report (2010): general assessment — no laws criminalising homosexuality, limited LGBT-specific protection. SUPERSEDED by freshness (rev 2026-09-27): sexual-orientation discrimination has been illegal since the 2018 constitutional equality reform, and current overviews describe no criminalisation; this archived report predates the reform. Fetch failed this pass (state.gov returned an error page), so no page-level claims were re-verified.

US State Department archived Human Rights Report (2015): no criminalisation, societal stigma reported without documented discrimination. SUPERSEDED by freshness (rev 2026-09-27): sexual-orientation discrimination has been illegal since the 2018 constitutional equality reform, and current overviews describe no criminalisation; this archived report predates the reform. Fetch failed this pass (state.gov returned an error page), so no page-level claims were re-verified.

freshness_all.fact: Sexual-orientation discrimination illegal since 2018 constitutional equality reform; no criminalisation described in current overview. The two archived 2010/2015 US reports predate that and are stale.

records.name: Marshall Islands
records.current_summary: The Marshall Islands demands real caution. Same-sex conduct legal; US-associated; no LGR; no documented anti-trans pattern; very thin data. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

sources.claim: Human Dignity Trust global criminalisation history: lists the Marshall Islands among the states that decriminalised same-sex conduct in the 2000s — "Marshall Islands (2005)" alongside USA (2003), Cape Verde (2004) and San Marino (2004) — i.e. no current criminalisation regime there.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Marshall Islands: significant problems were prison conditions, corruption and domestic violence; no reports of torture, arbitrary killings or disappearances - no LGBT-specific abuses reported.

Pacific Sexual & Gender Diversity Network Marshall Islands page: profiles Anfernee Nenol Kaminaga ("Nenol"), 25, a pansexual genderqueer Marshallese who co-created and led "Brighten the Rainbow", known as the first openly LGBTIQ initiative in the Marshall Islands; also a UNESCO Youth Ambassador and youth representative at the first UN Youth Climate Action Summit.

records.name: Republic of the Congo
records.current_summary: Republic of the Congo is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal (never criminalised); EUAA COI (2024) documents societal discrimination, police harassment, and absence of protection; no LGR; small underground community.

sources.claim: EUAA COI Query Response Q29 (May 2024) on the Republic of the Congo: systematic review of legislation, implementation, treatment by state and society, and availability of state protection for LGBTQI+ people. Key findings: no law criminalises consensual same-sex conduct between adults; Penal Code Article 331 (per ILGA) sets age of consent at 21 for same-sex vs 18 for different-sex acts; the under-21 'shameless act / against nature' provision's scope as applied to same-sex conduct is 'ambiguous', and sources say it is used to justify discrimination.

US State Department 2022 human rights report (Republic of the Congo), SOGI section: no law specifically prohibits consensual same-sex conduct between adults; a provision punishes 'shameless acts or acts against nature' with a person of the same sex under age 21 (6 months–3 years plus fine), scope ambiguous and not invoked for prosecutions. Police at times cite the provision to extract bribes from gay men; local NGOs reported violence, psychological/physical harassment, and financial extortion of LGBTQI+ persons by government and nonstate actors.

US State Department 2023 human rights report (Republic of the Congo): no known arrests or prosecutions of LGBTQI+ persons under the ambiguous under-21 provision during 2023; police continued using the 'act against nature' law as a pretext to solicit bribes from men; NGOs reported continuing psychological/physical harassment and financial extortion of LGBTQI+ persons by both government actors and nonstate actors, with no anti-discrimination protections in law.

freshness_all.fact: Homosexuality legal (2005 code removed criminalisation) but no protections, with documented discrimination/abuse — consistent with the EUAA 2024 query response cited.

records.name: Central African Republic
records.current_summary: Central African Republic is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but the state barely exists outside Bangui; armed groups control most territory; mob violence and police extortion against perceived LGBT people are documented; no LGR, no community infrastructure.

sources.claim: ILGA World 'Our Identities Under Arrest' (2023) - global report on laws criminalising LGBT people; the fetched copy contained no extractable text at research time (image-based PDF).

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report, Central African Republic: no legal anti-discrimination provisions for LGBTQI+ persons; marriage constitutionally defined as a 'union between one man and one woman' with same-sex marriage banned; legal gender recognition not permitted; LGBTQI+ persons cannot serve openly in the military; criminalisation of same-sex activity in public pushed the community underground, and there were no known organisations promoting LGBTQI+ human rights.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for the Central African Republic: documents extrajudicial killings, torture, rape by security forces and Seleka rebels, harsh prison conditions - general human-rights context with limited LGBT-specific content.

Erasing 76 Crimes / ILGA overview (20 May 2019): in the Central African Republic same-sex relations between consenting adults are not explicitly criminalised, but Article 85 of the criminal code criminalises 'attacks on public morals' — public same-sex acts carry harsher penalties than other moral offences. SOGI issues remain taboo and seen as 'imported from Europe'/'contrary to African values'; CAR received two UPR recommendations (SOGI non-discrimination, improving the situation of sexual minorities).

UN OHCHR summary of stakeholders' submissions for the CAR's UPR (45th session, Jan 2024): covers international obligations, national human-rights framework, institutional infrastructure - includes SOGI-related stakeholder recommendations.

freshness_all.fact: Current overview: same-sex acts legal, but public same-sex affection display criminalised — the 2019-2023 'Our Identities Under Arrest' era framing no longer matches; cited State Dept 2023 page superseded by newer code practice.
